events.credibility_reason: Minimality is not stated in any text the researcher read, and the authors hedge with 'may be the world's first'; the chapter itself was not read.
Undated, unsourced sentence seen only in search snippets, absent from the current article, with no grid or discoverer, and contradicted by the reported SudokuWiki 39 claim.
Known only from a search summary; the document text was unreadable, no proof or method is described, and it conflicts with the 40-given figure.

why: The statement asks for the maximum number of givens in a minimal (9x9) Sudoku. The 38- and 39-given puzzles are record constructions, so they are lower bounds on that maximum. Both date from before the snapshot and neither is digested. McGuire et al. and Tjusila et al. answer different questions: the global minimum of 17, and per-grid minima. Eppstein and Zhang is the only event after the snapshot. It studies the fewest clues needed for a given grid, which is a different quantity. Its 16x16 and asymptotic remarks about minimal clue sets are about other grid sizes and are the researcher's inference, so I answered it variant. The 40-given sentence cannot be dated and has no source. The SudokuWiki '39 is the most' claim has no argument behind it that the record can see, so I answered it none rather than treat it as an upper bound.
doubts: Whether the problem means only 9x9 grids or all n^2 x n^2 grids decides whether Eppstein-Zhang counts as variant. I read the statement as 9x9, as Wikipedia's sudoku context implies. Neither the 40-given record nor the SudokuWiki 39 claim was verified from primary text, and they contradict each other.
